Continuous probability distribution

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory Probability distribution
OurBigBook.com Words: 8k Articles: 82
A real probability distribution with a continuous cumulative distribution function assigns probability zero to each individual value. Here this is the broad meaning of continuous probability distribution. Many elementary examples are more specifically absolutely continuous probability distributions, described by a probability density function with respect to Lebesgue measure. Some texts use "continuous" for that narrower class. The Cantor distribution shows why the distinction matters: its cumulative distribution function is continuous, yet no probability density function with respect to Lebesgue measure represents its whole law. [ref].

Cantor distribution

Words: 66
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The Cantor distribution is the law of a random variable
X=∑n=1∞​3n2Bn​​,
(1)
where the Bn​ are independent Bernoulli random variables taking values zero and one with equal probability. Its values lie in the Cantor set, and its cumulative distribution function is the Cantor function. Every individual value has probability zero, but the Cantor set has probability one despite having zero Lebesgue measure. A probability density function on that set would integrate to zero, so it cannot describe this law. The example motivates the distinction between a continuous probability distribution and an absolutely continuous probability distribution.

Distance between two uniform points in a three-dimensional ball (fR​(r)=3r2/R3−9r3/(4R4)+3r5/(16R6))

Words: 128
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For two independent random variables taking values in a three-dimensional ball with constant volume probability density, the density of their distance is the displayed expression for 0≤r≤2R, and zero otherwise. Both independence and the common radius R>0 are essential. To derive it, put u=∣r1​∣, v=∣r2​∣ and integrate the product volume differential form over orientations. The law of cosines gives the angular Jacobian determinant v/(ur), leaving fR​(r)=9r∫uvdudv/(2R6) over 0≤u,v≤R, ∣u−v∣≤r≤u+v. With x=u+v, y=u−v, the integrand becomes (x2−y2)dxdy/8. Direct integration gives ∫uvdudv=2R3r/3−R2r2/2+r4/24. An independent geometric derivation uses the overlap volume of two radius-R balls displaced by r, namely π(4R+r)(2R−r)2/12, multiplied by 4πr2 and divided by the square of 4πR3/3. The density integrates to one and has mean 36R/35.

Beta-prime distribution (f(x)=B(a,b)(1+x)a+bxa−1​,x>0)

Words: 39
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
For a,b>0, this probability density function is obtained from a beta distribution variable U by X=U/(1−U). Indeed u=x/(1+x) and du/dx=(1+x)−2, and the change of variables formula gives the displayed density. In particular, the ratio of two independent equal-rate exponential distributions has a=b=1, density (1+x)−2 and cumulative distribution function x/(1+x).

Triangular distribution (Triangular(a,c,b),a<c<b)

Words: 144 Articles: 1
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A triangular probability density function rises linearly from zero at a to its mode c, then falls linearly to zero at b. Its peak is 2/(b−a). Its inverse transform sampling rule is a+u(b−a)(c−a)​ for u≤(c−a)/(b−a), and b−(1−u)(b−a)(b−c)​ otherwise.

Difference of two independent uniform random variables (U−V∼q(t)=(a−∣t∣)/a2,∣t∣<a)

Words: 108
Triangular distribution OurBigBook.com
If U,V are independent random variables, each with the uniform distribution on [0,a] for a>0, then T=U−V has the symmetric triangular distribution
q(t)={(a−∣t∣)/a2,0,​∣t∣<a,∣t∣≥a.​
(2)
The convolution of probability densities gives q(t)=a−2∫1[0,a]​(s)1[0,a]​(s+t)ds. The overlap of these two intervals has length a−∣t∣ for ∣t∣<a and is empty otherwise, proving the formula. By linearity of expectation and the variance of a sum,
E[T]=0,Var(T)=a2/6.
(3)
For 0≤b≤a, its upper-tail probability is (a−b)2/(2a2).
A useful model for elapsed time measured from two independently truncated clock readings uses a as the display resolution and T as the endpoint-offset difference. Independence is essential: uniform marginal probability distributions alone do not imply this triangular distribution. For example U=V gives T=0 with certainty. In general, with the same uniform marginals, Var(U−V)=a2/6−2Cov(U,V).

Arcsine distribution (Beta(21​,21​))

Words: 989 Articles: 4
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The standard arcsine distribution is a continuous probability distribution on [0,1] with probability density function
f(x)=πx(1−x)​1​,0<x<1.
(4)
It is the beta distribution with both parameters equal to 1/2. The density grows without bound toward both endpoints, yet neither endpoint has any probability mass. Its name comes from the inverse sine in its cumulative distribution function.[ref]
A useful way to see the shape is to choose a point uniformly around a circle and project it onto a diameter. Equal angular intervals do not give equal horizontal distances: the projection moves slowly near either end. An ideal harmonic oscillator sampled at a uniformly chosen time in one complete period has the same endpoint concentration after rescaling its position. The distribution translates a simple geometric slowdown into a precise probability calculation.
For an original comparison, take equal-length regions: the middle half [1/4,3/4], and the two outside quarters together. Then
P(1/4≤X≤3/4)=31​,P(X<1/4 or X>3/4)=32​.​
(5)
A uniform distribution on [0,1] instead assigns each region probability 1/2. Both distributions have mean 1/2; the mean alone hides their different concentration.

Arcsine distribution from a uniform angle (X=sin2Θ,Θ∼Uniform(0,π/2))

Words: 291
Arcsine distribution OurBigBook.com
Choose Θ with uniform distribution on (0,π/2) and set X=sin2Θ. Since the sine is increasing on this interval,
F(x)=P(X≤x)=π2​arcsinx​,0≤x≤1.
(6)
Differentiation gives f(x)=1/(πx(1−x)​), and F(0)=0, F(1)=1 prove normalization. This also evaluates the density's improper integral without treating its divergent endpoint values as infinite probability.
For the circle construction, instead choose Φ with uniform distribution on [0,2π) and put Y=cosΦ. Each −1<y<1 has two preimages in one revolution. The change of variables formula adds both contributions:
fY​(y)=2π1​1−y2​1​+2π1​1−y2​1​=π1−y2​1​.
(7)
The affine change of variables X=(1+Y)/2 gives the standard arcsine distribution. A single monotone-branch calculation without the second preimage would give only half the total probability.
The same geometry explains the ideal harmonic oscillator y(t)=Acos(ωt+ϕ), with amplitude A>0 and angular frequency ω>0. Choose T uniformly in any complete period of duration 2π/ω. Its oscillation phase modulo 2π is uniform, and Y=y(T) has density
fY​(y)=πA2−y2​1​,−A<y<A.
(8)
Near a turning point, ∣dy/dt∣=ωA2−y2​ is small, so a fixed position interval takes more time to cross. For the chosen amplitude A=2cm, exactly one third of the period is spent in ∣y∣≤1cm, and two thirds outside that central interval. These are calculations for an ideal sinusoid, rather than measured oscillator data.
The sampling assumption matters. Taking one observation every full period returns the same position each time. It does not produce this probability distribution. Uniformly random observation times and a fixed regularly spaced sampling scheme are different models; aliasing can conceal the motion altogether.
Paul Lévy used a related geometric construction in his work on stochastic processes: project a uniformly chosen point on a circle onto its diameter to divide a segment. The projection description appears explicitly in §5 of his paper, following its arcsine density calculation.[ref]

Endpoint concentration in the arcsine distribution

Words: 183
Arcsine distribution OurBigBook.com
An unbounded probability density function does not imply an atom. Here
P(X=0)=P(X=1)=0,P(0<X<ε)=π2​arcsinε​∼π2​ε​(ε↓0).
(9)
The last equivalence follows from arcsinu/u→1. The endpoint interval has much more probability than the same interval under a uniform distribution, whose value is ε, but its probability still tends to zero. This is an integrable singularity.
For example, the first 1% of the unit interval contains about 6.377% of the probability; the last 1% contains the same amount because the arcsine distribution is a symmetric probability distribution. Each exact endpoint still has zero probability. Density and interval probability answer different questions.
A numerical integration routine must respect these endpoint integrable singularities. The substitution x=sin2θ gives
f(x)dx=π2​dθ,0<θ<π/2.
(10)
It turns a difficult-looking density integral into a constant measure in angle. Integrating finite bins is also a faithful way to draw the distribution near its endpoints; sampling f(0) to make a bar height is not.

Arcsine quantiles and moments (Q(p)=sin2(πp/2))

Words: 159
Arcsine distribution OurBigBook.com
Inverting F(x)=p gives the quantile function
Q(p)=sin2(2πp​),0≤p≤1.
(11)
Consequently, inverse transform sampling uses X=sin2(πU/2) with U uniform on (0,1). The quartiles are (2−2​)/4, 1/2 and (2+2​)/4.[ref]
The first and third quartiles are about 0.1464 and 0.8536, so the central half of the probability spans about 0.7071 of the unit interval. Under a uniform distribution, its width would be 0.5.
The symmetric probability distribution gives E[X]=1/2. The angle representation gives a short calculation of the second moment:
E[X2]=π2​∫0π/2​sin4θdθ=83​,Var(X)=83​−41​=81​.
(12)
Use sin4θ=(3−4cos2θ+cos4θ)/8 to evaluate the integral. A uniform distribution on [0,1] has variance 1/12; the larger variance 1/8 quantifies the greater spread toward the ends.
More generally, for a nonnegative integer n, the beta function yields
E[Xn]=B(1/2,1/2)B(n+1/2,1/2)​=4n(n2n​)​.
(13)
For n=0 this is one; for n=1,2 it reproduces the values above. The central binomial coefficient thus appears in an exact moment calculation for a continuous probability distribution.

Arcsine distribution on a bounded interval (Y=a+(b−a)X,a<b)

Words: 128
Arcsine distribution OurBigBook.com
Specify whether two parameters mean endpoints or location and width. With endpoints a<b, define Y=a+(b−a)X for a standard arcsine distribution variable X. Then
fY​(y)=π(y−a)(b−y)​1​,a<y<b,FY​(y)=π2​arcsinb−ay−a​​.
(14)
This is a location-scale family with location a and width b−a. Its mean is (a+b)/2 and its variance is (b−a)2/8. A convention using parameters a,w for location and width instead has right endpoint a+w, so it must not be read as having endpoints a,w.[ref]
For example, a chosen interval [−2,6] gives mean 2 and variance 8, while its density still concentrates toward both endpoints. It is a bounded probability distribution; its endpoint singularities do not make its support infinite.

Pareto distribution (Pareto(α,β))

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The Pareto distribution describes a positive random variable whose tail probability falls as a power law. In the shape–minimum convention used here, X∼Pareto(α,β) has shape parameter α>0 and minimum β>0, with probability support [β,∞). Its probability density function is
f(x)={αβαx−α−1,0,​x≥β,x<β.​
(15)
The minimum β has the same units as X; the shape parameter α is dimensionless. At fixed α, changing β gives a scale family, since X/β∼Pareto(α,1). This convention is also used in uniform-Pareto conjugacy.[ref]
The survival function and cumulative distribution function are
F(x)=P(X>x)={1,(β/x)α,​x<β,x≥β,​F(x)=1−F(x).
(16)
For 0<p<1, solving F(x)=p gives the quantile function
Q(p)=β(1−p)−1/α.
(17)
Its right-hand limit at p=0 is β; it tends to infinity as p↑1.[ref] There is no probability mass at β: changing a probability density function's value at that single point changes no probabilities.
Choose α=2 and β=10 as an original theoretical example. Then P(X>20)=1/4, P(X>100)=1/100, the median is 102​≃14.142, and the 0.99 quantile is Q(0.99)=100. These chosen values and all figures below describe mathematical probability distributions, not actual wealth observations.
On this log-log plot, write r=x/β to obtain logF(βr)=−αlogr. The slope is −α, whereas the probability density function has power exponent α+1. Multiplying a threshold by ten divides its tail probability by 10α. A larger α therefore concentrates the Pareto distribution nearer β; a smaller α makes extreme values more plausible. This exact scaling is useful when modelling large positive losses or sizes over several orders of magnitude.
The Pareto distribution is a heavy-tailed distribution: for every t>0, the exponential moment E[etX] diverges because etxx−α−1 eventually grows without bound. In contrast, the Laplace distribution has exponentially decreasing tails and some finite positive exponential moments. The Student's t-distribution also has power tails, but on both sides of the real line, with a smooth central region rather than a positive minimum.

One-big-jump polynomial lower bound (P(Sn​≥na)≥P(X1​≥na))

Words: 103
Pareto distribution OurBigBook.com
Let Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, where the summands are independent and identically distributed with Pareto distribution Pareto(α,β). Their positivity implies {X1​≥na}⊆{Sn​≥na}, so for fixed a>0 and na≥β,
P(Sn​≥na)≥(naβ​)α,nα​lognaβ​≤n1​logP(Sn​≥na)≤0.
(18)
Both outer expressions tend to zero. A single large summand already prevents a strictly negative exponential rate. No positive exponential moment exists, so the exponential-moment form of the Cramér theorem cannot be applied. The bound proves this logarithmic rate and does not assert an exact tail asymptotic. In particular, it remains true when a lies below a finite mean, where the event need not even be rare. The stronger fixed-summand-count asymptotic in a heavy-tailed subexponential distribution is a separate statement.

Pareto moment threshold (E[Xq]=αβq/(α−q),0≤q<α)

Words: 211
Pareto distribution OurBigBook.com
A Pareto distribution is a proper probability distribution for every α,β>0, even when its mean is infinite. To see both facts, integrate the probability density function against xq. For real q≥0,
E[Xq]=αβα∫β∞​xq−α−1dx=⎩⎨⎧​α−qαβq​,+∞,​0≤q<α,q≥α.​
(19)
The improper integral converges exactly when q−α−1<−1. At q=α it diverges logarithmically; above that it diverges as a positive power of the upper endpoint. Setting q=0 gives one, proving normalization regardless of whether higher moments exist.
Taking q=1,2 and using Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2 when both terms are finite gives
E[X]=α−1αβ​(α>1),Var(X)=(α−1)2(α−2)αβ2​(α>2).
(20)
For 0<α≤1, the nonnegative random variable has expected value +∞; a centered variance about a finite mean is unavailable. For 1<α≤2, the mean is finite and the variance is infinite.[ref] A finite total probability and a finite expected value answer different questions.
At the chosen minimum β=10, α=3 gives E[X]=15, E[X2]=300 and variance 300−152=75, but an infinite third moment. At α=3/2, the mean is 30 and the variance is infinite; at α=3/4, even the mean is infinite, while the median remains the finite number 1024/3≃25.198. At the boundary α=2, the earlier example has mean 20 but infinite variance. A finite sample contains finite values almost surely; that fact cannot establish that the underlying mean or variance is finite.

Pareto tail conditional scaling (X∣X≥u∼Pareto(α,u),u≥β)

Words: 186
Pareto distribution OurBigBook.com
Conditioning a Pareto distribution on exceeding a threshold changes its minimum while preserving its shape parameter. For u≥β and x≥u, the definition of conditional probability gives
P(X>x∣X≥u)=(β/u)α(β/x)α​=(xu​)α.
(21)
Equivalently, for r≥1,
P(X/u>r∣X≥u)=r−α.
(22)
The ratio to the threshold has the same Pareto distribution at every admissible threshold.[ref] For the chosen α=2, β=10, only 1/4 of outcomes exceed 20, but among those outcomes the probability of exceeding 40 is again 1/4. When α>1, the same identity gives conditional expectation E[X∣X≥u]=αu/(α−1).
This multiplicative scaling differs from the additive memoryless property of an exponential distribution. Indeed Y=log(X/β) has exponential distribution of rate α, because P(Y>y)=e−αy for y≥0. Thus logarithms turn multiplication into addition and explain the scaling property. Conversely, if U has uniform distribution on (0,1), inverse transform sampling gives X=β(1−U)−1/α.
The excess Z=X−u conditional on X≥u has survival function (1+z/u)−α for z≥0. In the generalized Pareto distribution convention P(Z>z)=(1+ξz/σ)−1/ξ, this means ξ=1/α and σ=u/α. Here the excess starts at zero; the original Pareto distribution starts at β>0.

Pareto top shares and the 80/20 rule (T(q)=q1−1/α,α>1)

Words: 351
Pareto distribution OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative random variable with finite positive mean, the share of its total amount carried by the largest fraction q of outcomes can be defined by dividing their contribution to the expected value by the whole expected value. For a Pareto distribution, let 0<q≤1 and choose xq​=βq−1/α, so that P(X≥xq​)=q. If α>1, direct integration gives
T(q)=E[X]E[X1{X≥xq​}​]​=αβ/(α−1)αβαxq1−α​/(α−1)​=q1−1/α.
(23)
This is a share of amount, distinct from the fraction of outcomes. It depends on α, but not on the unit of measurement β.[ref]
For the chosen α=2, the top 20% starts at x0.2​=105​≃22.361 and carries T(0.2)=0.2​≃44.72% of the amount. To make the top 20% carry exactly 80%, solve
(1/5)1−1/α=4/5⟹α=log4log5​≃1.160964.
(24)
The resulting Pareto distribution has a finite mean and infinite variance. The 80/20 rule selects one shape parameter; it is not a universal law, or even a property of every Pareto distribution. For α≤1, the population-share definition above is unavailable because its denominator is infinite; substituting such an α into the finite-mean formula is invalid.
The left panel compares three quantiles in units of the minimum. The right panel shows T(0.2) only where the mean is finite, and marks the chosen 80/20 value. The thresholds α=1 and α=2 separate the moment regimes; they do not separate valid and invalid probability distributions.
A straight-looking empirical log-log plot does not by itself establish a Pareto distribution or a reliable tail exponent; estimating an exponent and assessing goodness of fit are separate tasks.[ref] If a Pareto distribution is used only above a fitted lower threshold, T(q) describes that conditional tail population, not automatically the whole population. A genuine finite upper cutoff gives a truncated distribution with finite nonnegative moments; its survival function, quantiles and top shares must be recalculated. Truncation is a modelling change, distinct from merely observing a finite sample. None of the chosen numbers here estimates an actual wealth distribution.

Rayleigh distribution (R∼Rayleigh(σ),σ>0)

Words: 961 Articles: 5
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The Rayleigh distribution is the probability distribution of the Euclidean norm of a two-dimensional random vector with independent zero-mean normal random variables of equal variance as components. If X,Y∼N(0,σ2) are independent, then
R=X2+Y2​∼Rayleigh(σ),fR​(r)={σ2r​e−r2/(2σ2),0,​r≥0,r<0.​
(25)
Here σ is the standard deviation of each component, not of the radius R. At σ=1 this gives the unit-scale probability density function re−r2/2.[ref]
This geometry turns two signed errors into one nonnegative distance. For example, suppose horizontal and vertical positioning errors are independent N(0,4cm2) random variables. Their means both vanish, but the distance from the intended point is usually positive. The Rayleigh distribution with σ=2cm gives the probability of landing inside any centered disk. These are chosen model assumptions, rather than measurements of a particular instrument.
An apparently paradoxical feature is that the most likely location per unit area is the origin, while the radial mode is σ. A narrow annulus farther out has more area. Near zero that growing circumference outweighs the falling planar density; farther out the exponential function wins. Distinguishing densities measured against different elements of area or length resolves the paradox.

Rayleigh radius from Gaussian components

Words: 148
Rayleigh distribution OurBigBook.com
The joint probability density of X,Y is
p(x,y)=2πσ21​e−(x2+y2)/(2σ2).
(26)
In polar coordinates, x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ, and the absolute Jacobian determinant is r. Thus the joint density of radius and angle factors as
pR,Θ​(r,θ)=σ2r​e−r2/(2σ2)2π1​,r>0,0≤θ<2π.
(27)
Integrating over angle gives the Rayleigh distribution. The same factorization shows that the angle has uniform distribution and is independent of the radius. This is a short change of variables argument: an annulus of width dr has area 2πrdr to first order.
The assumptions are substantive. Unequal component variances give elliptical rather than circular density contours; a nonzero mean displaces the center. Even zero covariance and equal normal distributions do not suffice without independence. For an original counterexample, let X∼N(0,σ2) and let S be an independent Rademacher random variable. Put Y=SX. Then Y has the same normal distribution as X, and Cov(X,Y)=E[SX2]=0. Nevertheless, all points lie on y=x or y=−x, and R=2​∣X∣ has density
fR​(r)=σπ​1​e−r2/(4σ2),r≥0,
(28)
which is positive at zero, unlike the Rayleigh distribution. This pair is not a Gaussian random vector.

(29)

rp​=σ−2log(1−p)​,0<p<1.​

Squared Rayleigh radius (R2/(2σ2)∼Exp(1))

Words: 118
Rayleigh distribution OurBigBook.com
Squaring a Rayleigh distribution variable produces an exponential distribution. For w≥0,
P(R2>w)=e−w/(2σ2),R2∼Exp(2σ21​),
(33)
where the exponential distribution parameter is a rate. Equivalently, R2/σ2 has chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom (statistics). An amplitude and its square therefore have different probability density functions, even though one determines the other.
This makes the Rayleigh-normal scale mixture transparent: at unit scale, R2 is exponential, allowing a random normal scale to produce a Laplace distribution. Another equivalent parametrization uses a Weibull distribution with shape two and scale 2​σ. Conventions that call this latter scale the Rayleigh scale differ by a factor of 2​; check the probability density function before comparing numerical parameter values.[ref]

Random-phase amplitude and the Rayleigh distribution

Words: 177
Rayleigh distribution OurBigBook.com
In an 1880 paper, John William Strutt, known as Lord Rayleigh, studied the resultant of many oscillations with a common frequency and arbitrary oscillation phases. His large-number calculation distinguished a mean intensity from a definite resultant amplitude and used planar coordinates followed by a polar integral. The resulting amplitude density is the Rayleigh distribution in a different scale convention. This is a large-number description, not an exact law for every finite collection of oscillations.[ref]
To see the connection in a chosen model, take independent oscillation phases Θj​ with uniform distribution on [0,2π) and equal component amplitude a. The phasor sum has coordinates
Xn​=a∑j=1n​cosΘj​,Yn​=a∑j=1n​sinΘj​.
(36)
Both have mean zero, variance na2/2 and zero covariance. The multivariate central limit theorem gives an approximately circular Gaussian random vector for large n, with σ=an/2​. Its amplitude Xn2​+Yn2​​ is therefore approximately Rayleigh. For every finite n, that amplitude is bounded by na, whereas a Rayleigh distribution has an unbounded tail. At n=1 it is exactly a. This simple endpoint check prevents the approximation from becoming a false exact identity.

A hypoexponential distribution is the distribution of a sum of independent variables with exponential distributions. For two positive unequal rates λ,μ, convolution of independent random variables gives the probability density function
f(s)=μ−λλμ​(e−λs−e−μs),s≥0.
(37)
It is zero for negative s. Its equal-rate limit is the shape-two gamma distribution with rate λ.

(38)
where the Ei​ are independent exponential random variables of rate λ. To see this, the first of N independent exponential clocks rings at rate Nλ; after it rings, the memoryless property leaves N−1 independent rate-λ clocks. The successive order statistic gaps are therefore independent with rates Nλ,(N−1)λ,…,λ. Their sum has the same distribution as ∑Ti​. In particular, for x>0, the tail at Nx has logarithm −λNx+o(N), since 1−(1−e−λNx)N∼Ne−λNx. The sum divided by N has a large deviation principle with speed N and rate function λx on x≥0, infinity otherwise.

Student's t-distribution (tν​,ν>0)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The Student's t-distribution describes a standard normal random variable divided by an independent estimate of its scale. For any real ν>0, let Z∼N(0,1) have the standard normal distribution and let V∼χν2​ have the chi-squared distribution, with Z and V independent. Then
T=V/ν​Z​∼tν​.
(39)
The parameter ν is called the number of statistical degrees of freedom. It need not be an integer: the chi-squared distribution is a gamma distribution with shape ν/2 and rate 1/2. The independence assumption is essential; specifying only the two marginal distributions does not determine the probability distribution of their ratio.
Its probability density function on the whole real line is
fν​(t)=νπ​Γ(ν/2)Γ((ν+1)/2)​(1+νt2​)−(ν+1)/2,−∞<t<∞,
(40)
where Γ is the gamma function. Every member is a symmetric distribution about zero. At ν=1 it is the Standard Cauchy distribution; as ν→∞ it approaches the standard normal distribution. The essential shape change is the tail: at any fixed finite ν, fν​(t) decays like a constant times ∣t∣−(ν+1), much more slowly than the standard normal density's exponential decay. Thus it is a heavy-tailed distribution. [ref]
The left panel shows the centers; the right panel uses a logarithmic scale to reveal the tails that a linear plot hides. All four curves have location zero and scale one. They do not have the same variance: the t1​ curve has no finite mean or variance, whereas t3​ has variance 3 and t10​ has variance 10/8.
More generally, the absolute moment E∣T∣p for p>0 is finite exactly when p<ν, as follows by comparing the tail integrand with tp−ν−1. Consequently
E[T]=0(ν>1),Var(T)=ν−2ν​(ν>2).
(41)
For 0<ν≤1 there is no finite mean; symmetry alone cannot supply one. For 1<ν≤2 the mean exists but the variance is infinite. For 0<ν≤1 even the centered definition of variance is unavailable because the mean does not exist.
A shifted and scaled version Y=m+bT, b>0, has probability density function b−1fν​((y−m)/b). The scale b is not its standard deviation: for ν>2,
SD(Y)=bν−2ν​​.
(42)
For example, ν=3 and scale b=2 give standard deviation 23​, rather than 2. The distinction matters when using a Student's t-distribution to model data with occasional extreme values, as well as when interpreting a Student t confidence interval.

Normal scale mixture representation of Student t (T=Z/Λ/ν​,Λ∼χν2​)

Words: 116
Student's t-distribution OurBigBook.com
For independent Z∼N(0,1) and Λ∼χν2​, the displayed ratio has the Student t-distribution with ν>0 statistical degrees of freedom. Equivalently, conditional on Λ=λ>0, T has normal distribution N(0,ν/λ). This is a normal scale mixture representation of Student t: a small latent denominator occasionally produces a much larger spread. The result is a heavy-tailed distribution even though every conditional probability distribution is a normal distribution.
For a short derivation, independence lets us multiply the conditional normal density and the chi-squared distribution's probability density function, then integrate over the unobserved λ:
fν​(t)=∫0∞​2πνλ​​e−λt2/(2ν)2ν/2Γ(ν/2)λν/2−1e−λ/2​dλ.
(43)
The resulting gamma function integral has shape (ν+1)/2 and rate (1+t2/ν)/2, yielding the normalized probability density function above. Also, for ν>2, conditional expectation gives E[T2]=νE[Λ−1]=ν/(ν−2). Thus unit scale does not mean unit variance. Finally, E[Λ/ν]=1 and Var(Λ/ν)=2/ν imply convergence in probability to 1 by Chebyshev's inequality; Slutsky's theorem then gives the standard normal distribution limit.

If Z∼N(0,1) and U∼χν2​ are independent, then (Z+δ)/U/ν​ has the noncentral t-distribution with ν>0 statistical degrees of freedom and noncentrality δ. It describes the test statistic of a Student's t-test under a shifted alternative hypothesis. At δ=0 it reduces to the Student's t-distribution. This is different from adding a constant to a central Student t-distribution: here the shift is inside the random denominator. For a normal distribution sample tested against null hypothesis μ=μ0​, the noncentrality is δ=n​(μ−μ0​)/σ.

Studentized normal sample mean (T=(Xˉ−μ)/(S/n​)∼tn−1​)

Words: 443 Articles: 1
Student's t-distribution OurBigBook.com
Suppose X1​,…,Xn​, n≥2, are independent and identically distributed with normal distribution N(μ,σ2), where the mean μ and standard deviation σ>0 are unknown. Define the sample mean and sample variance by
Xˉ=n1​∑i=1n​Xi​,S2=n−11​∑i=1n​(Xi​−Xˉ)2.
(44)
Under these assumptions,
Z=σn​(Xˉ−μ)​∼N(0,1),V=σ2(n−1)S2​∼χn−12​,Z and V are independent.
(45)
Substitution gives the exact ratio
V/(n−1)​Z​=S/n​Xˉ−μ​∼tn−1​.
(46)
The unknown σ cancels. The denominator S/n​ estimates the standard error of the sample mean; its sampling variability is precisely why the Student's t-distribution has wider tails than the standard normal distribution.
The crucial independence has a geometric explanation. Apply an orthogonal transformation to the standardized observations (Xi​−μ)/σ, choosing its first coordinate along (1,…,1)/n​. That coordinate is Z; the remaining n−1 coordinates are independent standard normal random variables whose squared sum is V. Their joint probability density factorizes because the transformation preserves the squared length. This also explains the loss of one statistical degree of freedom when estimating the mean. Uncorrelatedness alone would not establish the required independence for arbitrary data.
The result is exact for every n≥2 under the stated normal distribution model. A small sample size by itself does not justify it: a sample from an arbitrary probability distribution need not have the displayed chi-squared distribution or the necessary independence.

Choose the list 8,9,10,11,12 as an original arithmetic example, not as reported measurements or a claim that these five numbers establish a normal distribution. If such values were obtained under the assumed independent and identically distributed normal distribution model with unknown σ, then
n=5,xˉ=10,∑i=15​(xi​−xˉ)2=10,s2=410​=2.5,5​s​=0.5​.

The observations, the sample mean and the confidence interval all have different meanings. The bar estimates the population mean; it is not an interval intended to contain 95% of individual observations. In repeated independent samples of size five from the assumed normal distribution, 95% of intervals constructed using the exact t quantile cover the same fixed μ. This is not a 95% posterior probability that the fixed statistical parameter lies in this particular realized interval. Such a probability requires a separate Bayesian inference model.

F4​(t)=21​+43​a−41​a3,a=4+t2​t​.

History of Student's t-distribution

Words: 243
Student's t-distribution OurBigBook.com
William Sealy Gosset worked at Guinness as a chemist and brewer and developed methods of statistical inference for small samples. He published under the pseudonym "Student". His employment as a chemist is independently recorded by MacTutor; the Dictionary of Irish Biography identifies him as an applied statistician and brewer and explains the pseudonym policy. [ref] [ref]
The 1908 paper The Probable Error of a Mean appeared in Biometrika 6(1), pages 1–25, with the byline "Student". Its introduction identifies the uncertainty introduced by estimating a standard deviation from few observations and explicitly assumes a normal distribution. Sections II and III develop the relation between sample spread and the standardized sample mean. Its notation uses a sample spread with divisor n and calls the ratio z; with that convention, the modern T equals n−1​z. The modern exact independence argument is given under studentized normal sample mean. [ref]
Section VI describes a physical sampling check: 3,000 cards carrying existing paired measurements were shuffled, then divided into 750 groups of four. He compared observed frequencies of sample spread and standardized sample mean with theoretical frequencies. This was a check using finite, grouped, approximately normal distribution data; it did not prove exact calibration for arbitrary populations. [ref]

An absolutely continuous probability distribution on the real line has a probability density function f with respect to Lebesgue measure λ: for every Borel set A, P(X∈A)=∫A​f(x)dx. The probability density function and cumulative distribution function example under probability distribution illustrates this class.

Probability density function (fX​(x))

Words: 618 Articles: 10
Absolutely continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A probability density function represents probabilities as areas under a nonnegative measurable function. For a real random variable with an absolutely continuous probability distribution, it satisfies
P(X∈A)=∫A​fX​(x)dx,fX​(x)≥0,∫R​fX​(x)dx=1
(50)
for every Borel set A. Its height is probability per unit of the outcome variable, not the probability of that exact outcome. Thus a probability density function may exceed one, while the probability of a singleton is zero. NIST describes the interval-probability interpretation through integration. [ref].
For the example fY​(y)=2y on [0,1], fY​(0.8)=1.6, but P(Y=0.8)=0 and P(0.7<Y<0.9)=0.92−0.72=0.32. The cumulative distribution function is FY​(y)=y2 within that interval, connecting density height to the local accumulation rate.
Changing the scale changes the density height. If Z=100Y, then fZ​(z)=fY​(z/100)/100=z/5000 on [0,100]. At the corresponding value z=80, its height is 0.016, while P(70<Z<90)=0.32 is unchanged. The factor 1/100 compensates for the wider integration variable. This is a change of variables, not a change in the underlying probabilities.
A probability density function is determined only almost everywhere: changing its values on a Lebesgue measure zero set changes no probabilities. The Cantor distribution has no such representation, and a mixed probability distribution can have both a point mass and a density component, so differentiating its cumulative distribution function does not recover all its mass.

Competing exponential clocks OurBigBook.com
Let S,T be independent random variables with exponential distributions of respective positive rates α,β. Condition on T=t and use the survival function of S:
P(S−T>u)=∫0∞​βe−βte−α(t+u)dt=α+ββ​e−αu,u≥0.
(65)
At u=0 this is P(S>T). Dividing by that probability proves that the positive difference conditional on S>T again has an exponential distribution with rate α. The memorylessness of the exponential distribution persists after an independent competing event has already occurred. Replacing the difference by a negative sentinel when S≤T adds an atom of a measure of mass α/(α+β) at that sentinel without changing the positive tail.

Geometric sum of exponential variables

Words: 33
Exponential distribution OurBigBook.com
If N is geometric on {1,2,…} with parameter p, independently of unit-rate exponential variables Si​, then
∑i=1N​Si​
(66)
is exponential with rate p. Its moment-generating function is p/(p−θ) for θ<p.

Continuous uniform distribution (U(a,b))

Words: 365 Articles: 9
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
A continuous uniform distribution has constant density on its interval of support.

Coverage of antipodal points by a randomly oriented sector (P(both covered∣Φ=ϕ)=max(ϕ−π,0)/π)

Words: 59
Continuous uniform distribution OurBigBook.com
For a sector of width ϕ and an independent uniformly distributed central bearing, a specified bearing is covered with probability ϕ/(2π). Two antipodal bearings cannot both be covered when ϕ<π. For ϕ≥π, the allowable centre arcs overlap in two components of length ϕ−π, proving the displayed conditional probability. Averaging over the width's probability density function gives unconditional coverage probabilities.

Random quadratic with uniform coefficients (r2+2Vr+U=0)

Words: 65
Continuous uniform distribution OurBigBook.com
For independent U,V uniform on [0,1], real roots occur on U≤V2, a region of probability 1/3. On that region both roots are nonpositive. Both lie in [−1,0] exactly when max(0,2V−1)≤U≤V2. Its area is 1/12, so the conditional probability of both absolute values being at most one is 1/4. Joint probability density integration turns algebraic discriminant and root constraints into simple planar areas.

Uniform random variable (U∼U(a,b))

Words: 24
Continuous uniform distribution OurBigBook.com
A uniform random variable has a uniform distribution. Independent such variables can supply independent inverse transform sampling; reusing a single variable for two transforms generally creates dependence.

Steinhaus random variable (η=eiΘ,Θ∼Unif[0,2π))

Words: 84 Articles: 1
Continuous uniform distribution OurBigBook.com
A Steinhaus random variable is uniformly distributed on the complex unit circle. It can be generated as ϵcosθ+iδsinθ using independent signs ϵ,δ and an independent uniform angle θ∈[0,π/2]. This conditional sign representation transfers Rademacher sum inequalities to random complex phases.

Steinhaus first-moment lower bound (∑i​∣ai​∣2≤2(E∣∑i​ai​ηi​∣)2)

Words: 45
Steinhaus random variable OurBigBook.com
For independent Steinhaus random variables, condition on their acute angles and use the sharp Rademacher second-moment inequality on the 2d sign coefficients ai​cosθi​,iai​sinθi​. Their squared moduli sum to ∑i​∣ai​∣2 independently of the angles, so the conditional first moment is at least the same fixed square-root bound. Averaging proves the assertion.

The square of a uniform distribution variable on (0,1) has cumulative distribution function x​ and an integrable inverse-square-root probability density function. Reflection replaces x by 1−x in that density.

Exponential characterization by a uniform random split

Words: 49
Uniform split of a random total OurBigBook.com
Write h(y)=∫y∞​g(t)/tdt. The two pieces in a uniform split are independent exactly when
−h′(y+z)=h(y)h(z).
(70)
Setting z=0 shows that h(y)=ce−cy for some c>0. Thus the pieces are independent exactly when they are independent exponential variables of the same rate; equivalently, the total has gamma density c2xe−cx.

Laplace distribution (Laplace(μ,b),b>0)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Continuous probability distribution OurBigBook.com
The Laplace distribution, also called the double exponential distribution, is a location-scale family with probability density function
f(x;μ,b)=2b1​exp(−b∣x−μ∣​),x∈R,μ∈R,b>0.
(71)
The location μ is its mean, median and mode; b controls its spread. In the centred rate convention, the same law has μ=0 and θ=1/b>0, giving f(x)=θe−θ∣x∣/2. Keeping track of whether a parameter is a scale or its reciprocal prevents reversing the effect of increasing it. [ref]
The two halves of the probability density function are reflected exponential decay curves, each with total probability 1/2. Their meeting point has a sharp corner: the left and right derivatives are 1/(2b2) and −1/(2b2). This finite peak is not a positive probability mass at μ. Indeed
P(∣X−μ∣≤ε)=1−e−ε/b⟶0(ε↓0),
(72)
so P(X=μ)=0, just as for any absolutely continuous probability distribution.
The figure compares a Laplace distribution with μ=0, b=1 against a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation σ=2​: both have variance 2. The right panel uses a logarithmic scale for the two-sided tail probability P(∣X∣>r). Its straight Laplace distribution curve comes from e−r; the normal distribution tail falls faster. Thus values far from the center can be more plausible under a Laplace distribution even after matching the variance. These are theoretical curves, not measured frequencies. The tails still have exponential decay; this is not a heavy-tailed distribution in the convention requiring every positive exponential moment to diverge.
Integrating either half of the probability density function gives the cumulative distribution function
F(x)={21​e(x−μ)/b,1−21​e−(x−μ)/b,​x<μ,x≥μ.​
(73)
In particular F(μ)=1/2. The basic moments are
E[X]=μ,E∣X−μ∣=b,Var(X)=2b2,SD(X)=2​b.
(74)
Thus the scale is the expected value of the absolute distance from the center, and is not the standard deviation. [ref] A short way to obtain the moments is to note that R=∣X−μ∣ has an exponential distribution with rate 1/b: P(R>r)=e−r/b for r≥0. Integrating gives ER=b and ER2=2b2; the symmetric distribution gives the centered first moment zero.

Laplace location and scale maximum likelihood (μ​∈argmina​∑i​∣xi​−a∣,b=n1​∑i​∣xi​−μ​∣)

Words: 489 Articles: 1
Laplace distribution OurBigBook.com
Suppose X1​,…,Xn​, n≥1, are independent and identically distributed with Laplace distribution Laplace(μ,b), where b>0. For realized values x1​,…,xn​, the likelihood function and log-likelihood function are
L(μ,b)=(2b)−ne−S(μ)/b,ℓ(μ,b)=−nlog(2b)−bS(μ)​,S(a)=∑i=1n​∣xi​−a∣.
(75)
For fixed b, maximum likelihood estimation of the location therefore minimizes the sum of absolute losses. This connects the Laplace distribution to robust statistics: each observation contributes a cost growing linearly with its distance, whereas squared-error loss grows quadratically.
Why does a sample median minimize S? Between successive order statistics, moving a a little to the right increases each distance to a value on the left and decreases each distance to a value on the right. Hence the slope is the number on the left minus the number on the right. It changes from negative to positive at the middle. More precisely, if x(1)​≤⋯≤x(n)​, all minimizing locations are
argmina​S(a)={{x(m+1)​},[x(m)​,x(m+1)​],​n=2m+1,n=2m.​
(76)
For an even sample size, the objective is flat throughout the interval between the two central order statistics. The midpoint convention for the sample median selects one solution; it does not prove uniqueness. [ref] This is the finite-sample counterpart of median minimizes expected absolute loss.
If S(μ​)>0, maximizing over b>0 gives
∂b∂ℓ​=−bn​+b2S(μ​)​=0,b=nS(μ​)​.
(77)
The derivative is positive below this value and negative above it. Moreover the maximized likelihood function is proportional to S(μ)−n wherever S(μ)>0, so the same minimizing locations give the joint maximum-likelihood estimates. [ref] The scale estimate divides by n; this formula is not an assertion that it is an unbiased estimator.
The boundary case matters: if all observations equal c, choose μ=c. Then S(c)=0 and L(c,b)=(2b)−n→∞ as b↓0. There is no finite joint maximum-likelihood estimate in the parameter space b>0. In particular, this always occurs for n=1. Writing b=0 does not produce an admissible Laplace distribution.

Laplace median robustness example

Words: 178
Laplace location and scale maximum likelihood OurBigBook.com
Choose the five numbers 1,2,2,5,10 as an original illustration. Their sample median is 2 and their sample mean is 4. The sum of absolute losses at the sample median is
S(2)=∣1−2∣+∣2−2∣+∣2−2∣+∣5−2∣+∣10−2∣=1+0+0+3+8=12.
(78)
If these numbers were modeled as an independent and identically distributed Laplace distribution sample, the joint maximum-likelihood estimates would therefore be μ​=2 and b=12/5=2.4. Using the sample mean instead gives S(4)=14, so it does not maximize this likelihood function.
Now replace only 10 by 100. The sample median stays at 2, while the sample mean becomes (1+2+2+5+100)/5=22. The minimized sum of absolute losses rises to S(2)=102, and the fitted scale rises to b=102/5=20.4. Stability of the fitted location therefore does not mean stability of every fitted parameter.
The left panel subtracts each objective's minimum so the two absolute loss curves can be compared despite the different totals. The right panel tracks the sample mean and sample median as the largest chosen value changes. This is an outlier sensitivity illustration, not actual observations or a check that a Laplace distribution fits any population. In applications, regression residuals and the data-generating assumptions need separate examination; a stable sample median alone does not validate a statistical model.

Laplace prior for sparse images (π0​(u)∝e−λ∥u∥1​)

Words: 102
Laplace distribution OurBigBook.com
Independent centered Laplace distributions for pixel intensities give the prior distribution
π0​(u)=(λ/2)de−λ∑j=1d​∣uj​∣,λ>0.
(79)
This prior favors small intensities through its sharp peak at zero, while its tails permit isolated appreciable pixels. Its negative log density is an L1 norm penalty, so with a Gaussian likelihood a maximum a posteriori estimate minimizes a sum of squared residuals plus that penalty. A draw from this continuous prior has no exactly zero coordinate with positive probability; sparsity of a maximizing estimate and concentration of prior mass near zero are different statements. The product prior also does not encode spatial contiguity. Inverse transform sampling produces each coordinate from an independent uniform distribution by λ−1log(2U) for U≤1/2 and −λ−1log(2(1−U)) otherwise, ignoring the probability-zero endpoints.

Laplace regression

Words: 193
Laplace distribution OurBigBook.com
For linear regression with fixed predictor vectors Xi​, assume conditionally independent responses with a common scale b>0:
Yi​∣Xi​∼Laplace(XiT​β,b).
(80)
Each conditional median and mean is XiT​β. The log-likelihood function is −nlog(2b)−S(β)/b, so maximum likelihood estimation minimizes the sum of absolute regression residuals:
S(β)=∑i​∣Yi​−XiT​β∣.
(81)
This is least absolute deviations. With only an intercept, it reduces to the Laplace location and scale maximum likelihood problem, so a sample median is a fitted intercept. Provided the minimum S(β​)>0, the scale estimate is b=S(β​)/n; the conditional standard deviation is 2​b. If the scale is denoted σ instead of b, the conditional standard deviation is 2​σ.
Minimizing a sum of absolute losses does not automatically give a unique coefficient vector. Even an intercept-only fit to an even sample size can have an interval of solutions, and redundant predictor columns can introduce further nonuniqueness. If a fit makes every regression residual zero, the joint likelihood function is unbounded as b↓0, so there is no finite joint maximum-likelihood estimate with positive scale.
The linear growth of absolute loss limits sensitivity to an extreme response at fixed predictors compared with squared-error loss. It does not protect against every outlier: an extreme predictor can have large regression leverage. The numerical example above changes a response in an intercept-only problem, and makes no general claim of immunity to such predictor changes.
